title: IBM: "Quantum Computing Complements, Not Replaces, AI — Financial Firms Must Secure Control Over Decisions and Payments"
excerpt: At Korea Fintech Week 2026, IBM laid out a strategy for the financial sector that combines quantum computing with sovereign AI. IBM framed quantum…
content:
IBM presented a next-generation computing strategy to the financial sector that combines quantum computing with artificial intelligence (AI). Alongside its vision of quantum computers as acceleration engines added to high-performance computing (HPC) and AI infrastructure rather than replacements for existing systems, IBM also urged companies to retain control over decisions and actions in an era when AI agents carry out payments directly.

IBM Korea held a media session on the 26th under the theme "Quantum Computing, Sovereign AI and the Future of Finance" at Korea Fintech Week 2026, held at the aT Center in Yangjae-dong, Seoul. Pyo Chang-hee, Vice President and Head of IBM Quantum Enterprise Business for Asia-Pacific, and Kim Min-sung, Vice President and Head of Public Sector at IBM Korea, presented quantum computing use cases and the sovereign AI strategy, respectively.

Pyo assessed that finance, an industry that carries a large volume of uncertainty and combinatorial problems, has substantial room for quantum computing adoption. Asset management, securities trading, anomaly detection, and credit scoring and insurance were cited as representative applications. The principle is to use quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition, entanglement and interference in computation through qubits, which, unlike ordinary bits, hold the 0 and 1 states simultaneously.

Proof-of-concept results were also presented. British financial group HSBC, working with IBM, combined quantum computation with an existing AI model that predicts the probability of trade execution in the European corporate bond market, improving prediction performance by up to 34%. U.S. asset manager Vanguard used quantum and conventional computers in parallel in an experiment to optimize an investment portfolio of 109 bonds. IBM drew a line, however, noting that both cases were results under specific experimental conditions and do not mean quantum advantage has been proven across all financial operations.

The structure IBM emphasizes is a division of roles. Just as a central processing unit (CPU) handles general computation and a graphics processing unit (GPU) handles large-scale parallel computation, a quantum processing unit (QPU) would take charge of specific hard problems. "This is not about tearing down existing systems but about adding a quantum computer to the HPC or AI infrastructure you already use," Pyo said, describing it as "an engine that can cut cost and time by accelerating and refining computation."

As an extension of its so-called "quantum-centric supercomputing" strategy, IBM recently announced a joint research plan with Nvidia and the U.S. Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory. The plan calls for validating technology that reduces quantum computation errors by linking IBM's quantum processor Nighthawk with Nvidia's DGX B200 system.

The hardware roadmap is also specific. IBM said it will introduce a next-generation 520-qubit processor, Nighthawk r3, in 2027 and aims to realize a fault-tolerant quantum computer that reliably corrects errors by 2029. Nighthawk r3 is designed to support 10,000 quantum operations, and a plan to build a 1,040-qubit system by linking two processors was also discussed.

In South Korea, IBM's quantum computer at Yonsei University's International Campus was upgraded this month to Nighthawk r2, which supports 120 qubits and up to 7,500 quantum operations. IBM said this was the first time a Nighthawk r2 had been deployed at a customer site anywhere in the world. "We measure the utilization rate of Yonsei University's quantum computer every month, and it is very high at around 75-80%," Pyo said, calling it "a foundation for companies to use the latest quantum computing infrastructure without going abroad." IBM also signed a quantum computing systems integration partnership agreement with Beneta Korea in September.

The advance of quantum computers carries the shadow of decryption risk. Pyo forecast so-called "Q-Day" — the point at which existing public-key cryptography is rendered useless — as early as 2029 and no later than the early 2030s. "We previously expected the mid-2030s, but the timeline seems to be moving up," he said, stressing the need to move quickly on adopting post-quantum cryptography (PQC) in payments and authentication. The timing of Q-Day has not yet been fixed. The G7 cyber expert group published a PQC transition roadmap for the financial sector in January, and the Bank of England and British financial authorities also recommended this month that financial firms inspect their cryptographic systems and draw up transition plans. IBM proposed that South Korean financial firms also prepare in stages, starting by training two to three dedicated staff and identifying tasks where the technology can be applied.

The session also treated control systems for an era of AI agents making payments directly as a key agenda item. Sovereign AI is the concept of a company directly controlling its data, models and operating environment, and the explanation was that as AI evolves from chatbots that deliver information into entities that execute transfers and payments, the scope of control is expanding to "judgment" and "action."

Shinhan Card succeeded in a real transaction with Mastercard in March in which an AI agent booked transportation and completed payment. In a survey IBM presented, about a quarter of 510 companies were found to be running AI agents in live systems. The problem is where responsibility lies. If a customer instructs an AI to book a business trip flight and accommodation within 500,000 won (approximately $370) and the AI pays for an unwanted hotel, the parties involved differ at each stage of the transaction — the AI developer, the seller, the payment gateway (PG) and the card issuer — complicating disputes. That is why the conditions the customer set, the basis on which the AI selected a product, who approved the payment and whether the transaction could be halted must all be recorded.

Kim stressed that financial firms must retain control over four areas — data, technology, operations and AI — even when they use external AI services. They must be able to continue operations even if a service provider is replaced or an outage occurs, and they must be able to prove after the fact which model made a judgment and who approved it. "The core of sovereign AI is not owning every technology and model yourself, but maintaining control over data, technology and operations, as well as over AI's judgments and actions, no matter where or how AI is used," he said. "Especially in an industry like finance, which demands a high level of trust and accountability, we must design systems together that can trace and explain what AI did and control it when necessary," he added.

Noh Sung-ho, head of the AI Finance Center at the Korea Capital Market Institute, who took part in the same session, pointed out that even if financial firms adopt different AI solutions, sharing the same foundation models can expose them to the same risks simultaneously. If a foundation model or application programming interface (API) fails, operations at multiple financial institutions could halt all at once. While ultimate responsibility for AI decisions rests with financial firms, he assessed that in South Korea the criteria for identifying core technology suppliers and the scope of management remain unclear. He stressed that financial authorities and institutions should work together to map the entire technology supply chain — including not only directly contracted suppliers but also foundation models and infrastructure — and manage risk concentration.

Lee Min-seop, a division head at Beneta Korea, assessed that financial institutions see quantum computing simultaneously as an "all-purpose technology" and a "distant-future technology," and as a result are failing to find concrete applications. A three-stage adoption strategy — defining business problems, running small-scale proofs of concept (PoC), and cultivating specialized staff and organizations — was offered as an alternative. Rather than building quantum computers in-house, validating problems that existing systems cannot solve through cloud-based services and comparing results is the realistic approach, according to the explanation.

The announcement comes as computing demand in the financial sector surges with the spread of AI. IBM's two-pronged agenda is to position quantum computing not as a primary infrastructure right away but as an auxiliary resource for handling hard problems in specific areas, while at the same time managing the system risks that stem from dependence on the AI supply chain. For financial firms, the task is to carry out in parallel the work of moving proof-of-concept results into actual operations and the contract and architecture design needed to preserve the option of switching models and infrastructure.
